b: I am the manager of an independent auto service/repair shop with 10 employees. One of my employees, Charles, who is one my service advisors, was recently elected to the city council of a neighboring town. I knew he was running and had no concerns that if he was elected it would impact his job as the council meetings are twice a month at 7:00pm, well past scheduled work hours.

Yesterday Charles gave me a list of when he needs time off for his council duties. Even though he has not been sworn in yet, he was asked to attend city meetings, workshops, etc. so he can he can “hit the ground running” when he starts this position. It also sounds like he expects time off, in addition to those mentioned, for ground-breaking/ribbon-cutting ceremonies and when higher level political leaders and other dignitaries come to town after he takes office. The council position is not a full-time job.

I explained to Charles that he would need to use vacation time and follow the vacation guidelines such as requesting a week or more in advance and if the other service advisor is on vacation, his request will be denied. His response was that his requests fall under “civic duty time off” and shouldn’t need to use vacation time for the couple of hours he would need off. Plus, he said if the other service advisor is on vacation at the same time as when he would be gone, I can step in and cover. I already do this when one is on vacation and really couldn’t do it with both gone, even if it is only for a couple of hours.

Have you ever heard of this “civic duty time off”? Is it a thing? Our employee handbook covers National Guard and jury duty (paid time off with no vacation used) which is, I guess, is civic duty time off. But nothing about time off needed when you are an elected official. In the back of my head, I think Charles was assuming he would also be getting paid time off for his “duties.” We did have a former employee who was service technician and a volunteer fireman/EMT for the small town he lived in and he had permission to be late for work with no disciplinary action if he was/had been out on a call preventing him for coming to work on time. He was late for work due to this maybe two or three times in the six years he worked for us. So this may have also been a “civic duty time off” situation.

My initial opinion is that his council duties are attending the nighttime council meetings that don’t impact his work schedule with an occasional daytime meeting that he could use vacation time and the other meetings/appearances are PR “fluff.” Your thoughts?
Yeah, this is (mostly) not a thing.
“Civic duty time off” isn’t an official legal category, although it’s often used colloquially or as a corporate term to refer to time off for jury duty or to vote.

A company may choose to offer “civic duty time off,” but that doesn’t generally cover an employee’s responsibilities as an elected official. It’s for mandatory or universal obligations (again, like jury duty or voting) that cover short, time-limited events. Running for and holding an elected office is generally considered a voluntary personal pursuit.

A small number of states do require some employers to provide an unpaid leave of absence for employees to serve in elected offices, but those generally only apply to larger employers and they only cover state-level legislators and not local city council members so Charles wouldn’t be covered by that anyway. (That’s because state legislatures usually meet in full-day blocks for several consecutive months out of the year, whereas city councils typically meet in the evenings once or twice a week, which allows their members to maintain normal daytime jobs without needing a lot of time off.) The exception to that is Iowa, which requires employers that have 20+ employees to give unpaid leave to anyone elected to a municipal or county office to serve (but even if you’re in Iowa, the fact that you have fewer than 10 employees means this wouldn’t apply to you).

Your stance that Charles should use vacation time for daytime duties is reasonable. (I would avoid calling the ribbon-cutting stuff “fluff,” though! It may be, but it’s also reasonable for him to consider it part of his official duties. How we characterize it really isn’t relevant, though, and I wouldn’t get into arguing that piece of it. Just let him know he needs to use normal leave for it.) You might say something like, “We’re thrilled for you that you were elected and want to be as supportive as possible, but as a small business we’re not equipped to accommodate absences beyond what our vacation time policy makes available to you.” And if he pushes back on that, you could say, “I wish we could do more, but our staffing isn’t set up to make it possible. If that means the job no longer works well for you, I understand, but I hope we won’t lose you over it.”
